etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English slepen, from Anglian Old English slēpan (West Saxon slǣpan), from Proto-West Germanic *slāpan, from Proto-Germanic *slēpaną.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To rest in a state of reduced consciousness.
(idiomatic, euphemistic) To have sexual intercourse (see sleep with).
(intransitive, idiomatic) To be careless, inattentive, or unconcerned; not to be vigilant; to live thoughtlessly.

quote.citation: 1706 October 9 (Gregorian calendar), Francis Atterbury, “A Sermon Preach’d in the Guild-Hall Chapel, London, Sept. 28. 1706. Being the Day of the Election of the Right Honourable the Lord Mayor.”, in Fourteen Sermons Preach’d on Several Occasions. […], London:  […]  E. P. [Edmund Parker?] for Jonah Bowyer, […], published 1708, →OCLC, page 407:
quote.text: We ſleep over our Happineſs, Great as it is, and want to be rous'd into a quick and thankful ſenſe of it, either by an actual Change of Circumſtances, or by a Compariſon of our Own caſe with that of other Men.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, 1 Thessalonians 4:14, column 2:
quote.text: For if we beleeue that Ieſus died, and roſe againe: euen ſo them alſo which ſleepe in Ieſus, will God bring with him.

quote.citation: 1886 October – 1887 January, H[enry] Rider Haggard, She: A History of Adventure, London: Longmans, Green, and Co., published 1887, →OCLC:
quote.text: It was that of a man in advanced life, with a long grizzled beard, and also robed in white, probably the husband of the lady, who, after surviving her many years, came at the last to sleep once more for good and all beside her.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To be, or appear to be, in repose; to be quiet; to be unemployed, unused, or unagitated; to rest; to lie dormant.

quote.citation: c. 1596–1598 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merchant of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i], page 182, column 2:
quote.text: How ſweet the moone-light ſleepes vpon this banke, […]

definitions.definition: (computing, intransitive) To wait for a period of time without performing any action.
(computing, transitive) To place into a state of hibernation.

quote.citation: 2009, Mike Lee, Scott Meyers, Learn Mac OS X Snow Leopard, page 91:
quote.text: Even when you have reasons not to sleep the computer, it's still a good idea to sleep the display after a period of time.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, mechanics, dynamics) To spin on its axis with no other perceptible motion.

quote.citation: 1854, Anne E. Baker, Glossary of Northamptonshire Words and Phrases:
quote.text: A top sleeps when it moves with such velocity, and spins so smoothly, that its motion is imperceptible.

definitions.definition: (transitive, mechanics, dynamics) To cause (a spinning top or yo-yo) to spin on its axis with no other perceptible motion.

quote.citation: 1995, All Aboard for Space: Introducing Space to Youngsters, page 158:
quote.text: Yo-yo tricks involving sleeping the yo-yo (like "walking the dog" and "rocking the baby") cannot be performed in space.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English slepe, sleep, sleepe, from Old English slǣp (“sleep”), from Proto-West Germanic *slāp, from Proto-Germanic *slēpaz (“sleep”).

definitions.definition: (uncountable) The state of reduced consciousness during which a human or animal rests in a daily rhythm.
(countable, informal) An act or instance of sleeping.
(uncountable) Rheum, crusty or gummy discharge found in the corner of the eyes after waking, whether real or a figurative objectification of sleep (in the sense of reduced consciousness).

quote.citation: 1886, Peter Christen Asbjørnsen, translated by H.L. Brækstad, Folk and Fairy Tales, page 233:
quote.text: When she had rubbed the sleep out of her eyes and wept till she was tired, she set out on her way and walked for many, many a day, till she at last came to a big mountain.
But it ringsAnd we rise,Wipe the sleep out of our eyes […]

quote.citation: 2017, Adam J. Fisch, Neuroanatomy: Draw It to Know It, Oxford University Press, →ISBN:
quote.text: [...] and draw the medial canthus (aka medial commissure) at the medial extreme. Now draw the lacrimal caruncle at the medial corner of the eye, which produces whitish, oily fluid—it produces “sleep in the eye.”

quote.citation: 2019, Jahangir Moini, Anatomy and Physiology for Health Professionals, Jones & Bartlett Learning (→ISBN), page 780, entry "Medial canthus":
quote.text: The part of the eyelid that is the location of the lacrimal caruncle, which produces rheum or "sleep," the gritty substance often present when awakening.

definitions.definition: A state of plants, usually at night, when their leaflets approach each other and the flowers close and droop, or are covered by the folded leaves.

quote.citation: 1843, Joh Müller, John Bell, Elements of Physiology, page 808:
quote.text: The daily sleep of plants, and their winter sleep, present in this respect exactly similar phenomena […]
